newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar-Slow demand, good crops dull premiums.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar-Slow demand, good crops dull premiums.

text.p: Sugar markets in Asia remained dull and premiums slackened on a lack of offtake and healthy crops expected from China, Australia and Thailand, sugar traders in the region said on Wednesday.
"You could call the sugar markets dull, lacklustre or even sluggish," said a trader based in Hong Kong.

Traders in Hong Kong and Japan said Thai raw sugar premiums remained bearish this week on a lack of active buying in the region and would slide further without support from speculative or physical buying from China.

Premiums for Thai raw sugar for March/May delivery were quoted at around 0.65/0.80 cents per pound (bid/offer) over the most active March futures on New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) FOB basis.
January/March delivery was quoted at 1.00 cent over New York futures, while May/July were quoted at 0.60/0.80 cent over New York.
A sugar trader at Japan's Nissho Iwai Corp declined to comment on rumours that the firm was open for 24,000 tonnes of bulk sugar from Cuba for early January shipment.
Other trade houses were said to be seeking Cuban sugar for the Japanese market, but this could not be confirmed.

Japan's raw sugar imports in the first nine months of this year totalled 1.14 million tonnes against 1.21 million tonnes during the same period last year, Finance Ministry data released last week showed.
"All we need now is Chinese buying. If not, the Thai premium is likely to ease further," a sugar trader at a major Japanese trade house said.
Premiums for the March/May deliveries would be supported at 0.50 cent in the near term, he said.
But traders in Hong Kong maintained that China would stay out of the import market until the first quarter of 1997, given the new crop was expected on the market by the end of November.
A Chinese sugar trader based in Beijing said China was still negotiating its 1997 contract for Cuban imports, although around 300,000 tonnes of Cuban sugar had been shipped in 1996.

Sugar crushing in China's southern province of Guangxi was proceeding according to schedule, according to a source based in China. But a senior Hong Kong trader said parts of Guangxi's crop had suffered minor damage from typhoons in September.
China's sugar output is officially forecast at 6.53 million tonnes, up from 5.53 million tonnes last year.
Australia's 1996 sugar crop was forecast by millers at 5.3 million tonnes, up from 4.99 million tonnes last year.

In Hong Kong, premiums over the New York market for sugar from South Korea -- which meets more than 70 percent of the colony's requirements -- had also dropped to about $150 per tonne C and F Hong Kong from $155-160 a week or two ago, traders said. --Mishi Saran, Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6358 --Eiichiro Tokumoto, Tokyo Commodities Desk (81-3) 3432 7391
